analyses.title: MAILEX: Email Event and Argument Extraction
analyses.research_question: Can event triggers and their structured arguments be extracted reliably from conversational workplace email threads despite shared triggers, long non-entity arguments, and dependencies on preceding messages?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct MAILEX from Enron email threads and define a taxonomy containing 10 event types and 76 argument roles covering requests, deliveries, amendments, data, meetings, and actions. They annotate 1,500 multi-message threads containing 3,936 emails and 8,392 event instances, then evaluate sequence-labeling, conditional-generation, and few-shot large-language-model approaches. Experiments include gold-trigger settings, ablations without conversation history, and qualitative error analysis of trigger and argument extraction.

key_findings.finding: MAILEX provides an authentic workplace-email event extraction benchmark derived from Enron, with event roles that include people or members, dates, times, and action-related information.
End-to-end argument extraction remains difficult: the reported argument-classification F1 is 0.368 for the BERT sequence-labeling system and 0.363 for the BART generation system.
Providing gold triggers substantially improves argument extraction, showing that trigger errors propagate strongly into downstream argument prediction.
Conversation history is useful: removing preceding emails lowers trigger and argument scores, and manual inspection found that 11 of 50 sampled emails required information from an earlier turn.
Shared or discontinuous trigger realizations and long non-named-entity arguments are recurring failure modes for the evaluated models.

Argument scoring permits partial span matching rather than requiring exact argument-span identity, so the benchmark does not directly enforce the exact evidence-span criterion needed for strict provenance-oriented extraction.
Few-shot text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo perform far below the fine-tuned models, with error analysis also identifying fabricated, missing, and span-mismatched arguments.

limitations: Conversation history is represented mainly by straightforward concatenation rather than a dedicated retrieval, selection, or memory mechanism.
The event taxonomy contains person/member and temporal roles, but the paper does not define a dedicated evaluation for implicit assignees versus explicit assignees or for group-assignee resolution.
The benchmark contains temporal arguments, but it does not isolate action-to-deadline binding as a separate benchmark task or metric.
Argument evaluation allows partial overlap, which is weaker than exact evidence-span evaluation.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not modeled as a general compositional scope-extraction problem.
The corpus is drawn from Enron and therefore represents one historical organizational setting rather than a broad sample of present-day enterprise email and chat.
The authors note unresolved difficulties with long non-named-entity arguments, sequential event dependencies, and effective use of conversational history.
raw_claims: MAILEX is built from conversational email threads in the Enron corpus.
The taxonomy contains 10 event types and 76 argument roles.
The annotated dataset contains 1,500 threads, 3,936 emails, and 8,392 event instances.
BERT sequence labeling obtains an end-to-end argument-classification F1 of 0.368.
BART conditional generation obtains an end-to-end argument-classification F1 of 0.363.
Gold event triggers produce much higher argument scores than predicted triggers.
Removing conversational history reduces extraction performance.
Eleven of fifty manually sampled emails were judged to require information from an earlier turn.
Models have difficulty with shared trigger spans and long non-named-entity arguments.
Argument evaluation gives credit for partial span matches instead of requiring exact matching.
Few-shot GPT-family systems perform substantially below the supervised BERT and BART systems on this benchmark.
The released resources include code and data.

analyses.title: Computable Contracts by Extracting Obligation Logic Graphs
analyses.research_question: Can contractual obligations and their semantic dependencies be extracted from natural-language contracts into a structured graph representation suitable for downstream conversion into executable code?
analyses.methodology: The paper introduces the Obligation Logic Graph, or OLG, as a representation of entities, relations, formulas, and dependencies among contractual obligations. It frames OLG construction as a joint entity-and-relation extraction problem and introduces Contract-OLG, containing 1,876 contract provisions, 18,597 entities, and 18,170 relationships. The accessible abstract reports experiments with Transformer-based and graph-based models and comparison against human experts, but it does not expose enough detail to reconstruct the architectures, annotation procedure, or numerical evaluation results.

key_findings.finding: The work introduces a structured graph representation intended to preserve contractual obligations and dependencies between obligations rather than extracting isolated entities alone.
Contract-OLG is reported to contain 1,876 contract provisions, 18,597 entities, and 18,170 relationships.
The extraction problem is formulated jointly over entities and relations, which is relevant to tasks that must bind an action or obligation to its associated participants and qualifiers.
The abstract reports a substantial gap between machine systems and human experts, particularly for relation extraction.
The accessible abstract does not establish that the benchmark specifically distinguishes implicit assignees from explicit assignees or evaluates group assignee resolution.
The accessible abstract does not establish dedicated evaluation of action-to-deadline binding, condition or negation scope, or exact textual evidence spans.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible during this review, so detailed annotation guidelines, model configurations, metrics, and error analyses could not be verified.
The domain is legal contracts rather than workplace email or enterprise chat.
The abstract does not provide evidence that implicit assignees, group assignees, or workplace conversational context are represented explicitly.
The abstract does not establish whether temporal expressions are bound to individual obligations as deadlines.
The abstract does not establish whether condition, negation, and modality scope are separately annotated or evaluated.
Exact textual evidence-span requirements cannot be verified from the accessible abstract.
Public availability of code and dataset files could not be established from the accessible source.
raw_claims: The paper proposes converting natural-language contracts toward executable representations through Obligation Logic Graph extraction.
An OLG captures entities and relationships associated with contractual obligations.
Dependencies between obligations are part of the proposed representation.
OLG extraction is formulated as a joint entity and relation prediction problem.
Contract-OLG contains 1,876 contract provisions.
The dataset is reported to contain 18,597 entities.
The dataset is reported to contain 18,170 relationships.
Transformer-based and graph-based approaches are evaluated.
The abstract reports that machine performance remains below human-expert performance.
Relation extraction is identified as a particularly difficult component.

analyses.title: Modality and Negation in Event Extraction
analyses.research_question: Can an open-domain event extractor distinguish events that happened, did not happen, or remain uncertain by modeling negation, modality, conditionality, counterfactuality, and propositional attitudes with syntactic scope?
analyses.methodology: The authors build MoNTEE, a lexicon-driven event extraction system on top of CCG parsing and dependency structures. Event relations are extracted together with modality tags generated from lexical triggers and graph paths intended to follow syntactic scope; phenomena include explicit negation, lexical negation, modal operators, conditionals, counterfactuals, and propositional attitudes. The method is evaluated intrinsically on 100 manually labeled event relations and then applied at scale to general, political, and sports news collections.

key_findings.finding: MoNTEE represents several kinds of event uncertainty rather than treating all extracted events as factual, including explicit and lexical negation, modal operators, conditionality, counterfactuality, and propositional attitudes.
The system uses dependency paths from modality triggers to events as a mechanism for approximating syntactic scope.
On the 100-relation intrinsic evaluation, the three-way happened/uncertain/did-not-happen classification achieves micro-F1 of 0.81 and macro-F1 of 0.76.
The paper explicitly excludes implicit negation from its treatment of negation, limiting coverage of pragmatically implied negative meaning.
The authors identify missing discourse context as an important limitation because modality can depend on surrounding text rather than only the local sentence.
The evaluated data are news articles rather than workplace email or enterprise chat, so performance does not establish robustness for conversational work communication.

limitations: The experiments use news text, not authentic workplace email or enterprise chat.
Implicit negation is explicitly outside the modeled negation coverage.
The system does not incorporate broader discourse context even though the authors note that modality can be context dependent.
The intrinsic manually labeled test contains only 100 event relations and has limited representation of some classes.
The CCG parser is trained for news-style English and may degrade on out-of-domain language such as conversational questions.
The task does not model assignee resolution, group assignees, or action-to-deadline binding.
Argument extraction is not evaluated as an exact evidence-span provenance task.
Only English is addressed.
raw_claims: MoNTEE classifies extracted events according to whether they happened, did not happen, or are uncertain.
The modeled phenomena include negation, lexical negation, modality, conditionals, counterfactuals, and propositional attitudes.
CCG dependency structure is used to connect modality triggers with events in their syntactic scope.
Implicit negation is not handled by the proposed system.
Two authors annotated 100 event relations for the intrinsic evaluation.
The annotators achieved a reported kappa of 0.77.
The system obtains micro-F1 of 0.81 and macro-F1 of 0.76 on that evaluation.
Large-scale analysis is performed on general, political, and sports news.
Modal operators constitute a large share of the detected non-factual-event phenomena.
The authors identify absence of wider context as an important limitation.
The implementation is publicly linked from the paper.

analyses.title: Summarizing Decisions in Spoken Meetings
analyses.research_question: How effectively can decision-related utterances in multi-party meetings be clustered by decision and summarized using dialogue-act-level or token-level supervised and unsupervised methods?
analyses.methodology: The work uses the AMI meeting corpus and assumes decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified. It first clusters decision-related utterances belonging to the same decision using TF-IDF or LDA-based unsupervised methods and supervised classifiers, then generates extractive summaries at the dialogue-act or token level with optional discourse context. Cluster quality is evaluated with clustering measures and summary quality with ROUGE against human decision abstracts.

key_findings.finding: Decision-related dialogue acts can be distributed and interleaved across a meeting, motivating an explicit clustering stage before decision summarization.
Supervised clustering performs better than the reported unsupervised LDA clustering on B-cubed F1, although the LDA method remains competitive for downstream summary quality.
With automatically produced clusters, an unsupervised LDA-based clustering pipeline can yield decision-summary quality comparable to the supervised clustering alternative.

When true decision clusters are supplied, supervised token-level summarization with discourse context achieves the strongest reported supervised configuration and approaches the paper's extractive upper bound more closely than automatic-cluster conditions.
The AMI data are scenario-driven four-person design-team meetings rather than authentic enterprise email or chat logs.
The task summarizes decisions but does not provide structured evaluation of assignee, deadline, condition, negation, modality, or exact argument evidence spans.

limitations: The corpus consists of scenario-driven spoken design meetings rather than naturally occurring enterprise email or chat.
The system assumes that decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified, so decision detection itself is outside the evaluated pipeline.
The output is decision summarization rather than structured extraction of action, assignee, deadline, condition, or decision arguments.
Implicit and group assignees are not defined as dedicated annotation targets.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not separately annotated or evaluated.
ROUGE-based summary scoring does not enforce exact evidence spans for individual structured arguments.
Some clustering stopping thresholds are manually selected.
raw_claims: The work targets concise summaries of individual decisions made during meetings.
Decision-related dialogue acts associated with one decision may be separated by other discussion.
The experiments use the AMI meeting corpus.
AMI contains scenario-driven meetings involving four participants playing design-team roles.
The experiments assume decision-related dialogue acts have already been identified.
The pipeline separately studies clustering and summarization.
Both unsupervised and supervised clustering approaches are evaluated.
Both dialogue-act-level and token-level summary selection are investigated.
Human-written decision abstracts provide the summary reference.
Automatic clustering substantially constrains downstream summary quality compared with true decision clusters.
ROUGE is used to assess generated decision summaries.

analyses.title: Document-Level Event Argument Extraction by Conditional Generation
analyses.research_question: Can document-level event arguments be extracted more accurately by generating filled event templates conditioned on the entire document rather than classifying candidate argument spans independently?
analyses.methodology: The authors formulate event argument extraction as conditional generation using event templates and encoder-decoder models such as BART, while constraining generated argument tokens to come from the input document. They introduce WikiEvents, a document-level event dataset with event and coreference annotation, and evaluate on both WikiEvents and RAMS using argument identification and classification metrics. The study also distinguishes ordinary argument extraction from informative-mention extraction and includes zero-shot transfer experiments across event types.

key_findings.finding: Template-conditioned BART generation outperforms the compared extraction baselines on both RAMS and WikiEvents for document-level event argument extraction.
The paper reports gains of 7.6 F1 on RAMS and 5.7 F1 on WikiEvents over the next-best compared systems, with a 9.3 F1 improvement for informative argument extraction.
WikiEvents evaluates argument heads by matching annotated offsets, while an alternative coreference-aware score gives credit when the predicted mention is coreferential with the reference argument.
Informative argument extraction deliberately prefers more informative mentions, such as names over nominal mentions and pronouns, which often requires selecting arguments farther from the trigger.
The authors identify remaining errors in which mutually exclusive semantic roles are both predicted and note that commonsense reasoning is needed for some implicit arguments.
The benchmark is built from Wikipedia and linked news material rather than workplace communication, and it does not define dedicated assignee-to-action or deadline-to-action relation targets.

The paper provides stronger span-grounding evaluation than summary-based benchmarks, but its coreference-aware metric deliberately relaxes exact mention identity and its head metric is not equivalent to requiring the complete evidence span for an argument.

limitations: WikiEvents is based on Wikipedia and news sources rather than authentic workplace email or enterprise chat.
The ontology is general event extraction and does not define implicit assignee, group assignee, or action-to-deadline binding as dedicated benchmark dimensions.
Head-offset evaluation checks an argument head rather than the complete textual evidence span.
Coreference-aware evaluation intentionally accepts a coreferential alternative mention, so it is less strict than exact evidence-span evaluation.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are not modeled as dedicated structured outputs.
The error analysis identifies unresolved ontological-role consistency problems and cases requiring commonsense knowledge for implicit arguments.
Document-level context can distract some baseline systems, indicating that simply enlarging context does not solve argument binding.
raw_claims: The approach casts document-level event argument extraction as conditional generation from an event template.
The generator is constrained so that argument tokens originate from the input document.
WikiEvents provides document-level event and coreference annotation.
The WikiEvents split contains 206 training documents, 20 development documents, and 20 test documents.
The dataset uses 67 event types from the KAIROS ontology.
BART-based conditional generation improves over the compared baselines on RAMS and WikiEvents.
The paper reports a 7.6 F1 gain on RAMS and a 5.7 F1 gain on WikiEvents relative to the next-best systems.
Informative argument extraction yields a reported 9.3 F1 gain over the strongest compared baseline.
Informative argument mentions are often substantially farther from event triggers than the nearest mention.
Head F1 uses reference offsets, whereas Coref F1 can accept a coreferential mention.
The error analysis finds mutually exclusive role predictions and cases where implicit arguments require commonsense reasoning.
Code, data, and related resources are publicly released.
